title: Mishima: Morning Mist
recordTitle: Mishima: Morning Mist (Mishima, asagiri), from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido Road (Tokaido gojusan tsugi no uchi)," also known as the Hoeido Tokaido

altText: A Japanese woodblock print of travelers at dawn. Figures, a horse and rider, and a palanquin carried on poles move past dark silhouettes of huts and trees, all softened by pale morning mist.

context: Utagawa Hiroshige made this print around 1833-34 as part of his series on the Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido Road, also known as the Hoeido Tokaido. The Tokaido was the road that linked Edo (now Tokyo) and Kyoto, and Mishima was one of its stations. The Art Institute's record offers no description beyond the basic data and a short image description.

descriptions.k: It is early morning. Mist floats over a road. Travelers walk. A person rides a horse. Men carry a box on poles. Dark huts and trees stand in the mist. Can you find the horse? Can you find the travelers?
descriptions.g12: This Japanese print shows an early morning on a long road. Soft mist hides the huts and trees. Travelers walk, someone rides a horse, and men carry a special seat on poles. Look at the dark shapes and the pale mist. What do you hear in the quiet morning?
descriptions.g35: Utagawa Hiroshige made this print around 1833 or 1834. It is one of a series of pictures of the stations along the Tokaido, the road between Edo and Kyoto. Here travelers start their day in the morning mist, with a horse and rider and a seat carried on poles, called a palanquin. Look at the black huts and trees. How does the artist use dark and light to show the mist?
descriptions.g68: Hiroshige's Mishima: Morning Mist is part of a series on the Tokaido Road, which connected Edo and Kyoto. Travelers, a horse and rider, and a palanquin carried on poles pass dark silhouettes of huts and trees. The mist is suggested by pale, soft color and by what is hidden. How does the artist suggest weather and time of day with so few details? What is lost and gained by showing the huts only as shadows?
descriptions.g910: In this Hoeido Tokaido print, c. 1833/34, Hiroshige renders dawn travel with a limited tonal range: pale mist, dark silhouetted huts and trees, and small groups of walkers, a horse, and a palanquin. Atmosphere replaces detail, a hallmark of his landscape prints. The Art Institute gives no further description. How do silhouette, tone gradation, and the placement of figures shape a mood of early-morning quiet, and how did the woodblock process make such effects possible?
descriptions.g1112: Mishima: Morning Mist exemplifies the ukiyo-e landscape tradition as renewed by Hiroshige's Tokaido series, which paired travel itineraries with atmospheric observation. Gradations of tone, dark silhouettes and spare figures evoke dawn and weather through carefully carved and printed blocks. The record offers only data and a short image description, so interpretation rests on the print itself. How do atmosphere, anonymity of travelers, and the logic of a series about a road together shape what the image communicates?

teacherNote.context: Part of Hiroshige's Hoeido Tokaido series, c. 1833/34, showing the station of Mishima on the road between Edo and Kyoto. The record gives only basic data and a short image description, so classroom discussion should rely on close looking.
directions: Have students make a simple stencil or cut-paper silhouette landscape, then add a wash of pale color to suggest mist.
Ask students to map a familiar route and decide which five places they would put in a print series about it.
Discuss how a print can hold information from several people, such as the artist, carver, and printer.
